fields.title: The Letter to the Ephesians
fields.subtitle: Pros Ephesious, “To the Ephesians”
fields.description: Paul’s letter of the church, written in chains and probably carried from one congregation of Asia to the next. It opens in a long outpouring of praise for every blessing in Christ, prays for eyes to see it, and tells Gentile readers who were once dead in their trespasses that God, rich in mercy, has made them alive: “it is by this grace that you have been saved, through faith.” Christ has broken down the wall between Jew and Gentile and made one new humanity, a body, a household, a temple; and so the letter turns to how such a people lives, in unity and truth, as children of light filled by the Spirit, in marriage and household, and armoured in God’s strength. In the Open Word Bible, a new translation from the Greek given freely to the public domain, with an introduction to the letter’s shape and meaning and a conclusion on where to read next.

qa.question: What is the Letter to the Ephesians?
qa.answer: The tenth book of the New Testament, a letter of the apostle Paul to the Christians of Ephesus and probably of other churches in the Roman province of Asia. Its first three chapters praise God for what he has done in Christ: choosing and redeeming his people, raising the spiritually dead to life by grace, and making Jews and Gentiles into one body. Its last three chapters show how that people is to live, beginning with the call to “live in a way that is worthy of God’s call” (4:1).

qa.question: Who wrote Ephesians, and when?
qa.answer: The letter names the apostle Paul as its author and speaks of him as a prisoner (3:1; 4:1; 6:20). The church has always received it as his, usually dated to his imprisonment in Rome around AD 60–62, when Tychicus carried it together with Colossians (6:21–22). Many modern scholars think it was written after Paul’s death by a disciple who knew his letters well, pointing to its style and its close dependence on Colossians; many others defend Paul’s authorship. Either way it gathers up his gospel as a whole.

qa.question: Was Ephesians written to the church in Ephesus?
qa.answer: Probably to Ephesus and beyond. Paul spent about three years in Ephesus (Acts 20:31), yet the letter sends no personal greetings and speaks of the readers’ faith as something he has heard about (1:15). Some of the oldest manuscripts lack the words “in Ephesus” in 1:1, and in the second century Marcion called it the letter to the Laodiceans. Many readers think it was a circular letter for the churches of Asia, with Ephesus as the chief among them.

qa.question: What does Ephesians 2:8–9 mean by being saved by grace through faith?
qa.answer: That salvation is God’s free gift and not a reward for anything we have done: “None of this comes from you; it is God’s gift,” and so “there is no room for anyone to boast.” Paul has just described his readers as dead in their trespasses and made alive by a God rich in mercy. But he goes straight on to say that God created us in Christ Jesus “for good works” (2:10), so that grace is the root of a changed life, not a substitute for one.

qa.question: What does Ephesians teach about wives and husbands?
qa.answer: Ephesians 5:21–33 calls believers to submit to one another in the reverent fear of Christ, asks wives to submit to their husbands as to the Lord, and asks husbands to love their wives the way Christ loved the church and handed himself over for her. Paul says marriage points to “Christ and the church” (5:32). Christians differ over how to apply it: some see the husband’s self-giving headship as a lasting pattern, others see mutual submission as the governing idea, transforming the household customs of Paul’s day from within.

qa.question: Which translation of the Bible is this?
qa.answer: The Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Greek and dedicated to the public domain, printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. The reasoning behind each of its sentences, with the Greek beside it, is published at openwordbible.org. The introduction and conclusion were written for this edition.

fields.title: Introduction
fields.body_html:
For it is by this grace that you have been saved, through faith. None of this comes from you; it is God’s gift. It is not the result of what anyone has done, so there is no room for anyone to boast. For we are God’s own work. In Christ Jesus he created us for good works, which God made ready in advance so that we would live our lives doing them.

— Ephesians 2:8–10

Most of Paul’s letters were written into the middle of a quarrel. Someone at Corinth has asked a question, the Galatians are being talked into circumcision, the Thessalonians are grieving and confused. Ephesians is different. There is no crisis in it, no rival teacher named, no list of friends to greet. For three chapters Paul hardly argues at all. He blesses God, he prays, he marvels, and then he tells a church how to live in the light of what he has marvelled at.

Readers have loved it for exactly that reason. Samuel Taylor Coleridge called it one of the divinest compositions of man. It is the letter of the church: of Jews and Gentiles made into one people, of a body with Christ as its head, of a household and a temple and a bride. And it was written, the letter says three times, by a man in chains.

Ephesus and the churches of Asia

Ephesus was the chief city of the Roman province of Asia, on the western coast of what is now Turkey: a harbour, a great theatre, and the temple of Artemis, one of the wonders of the ancient world. Paul stayed there longer than anywhere else on his travels. Acts tells of two years of daily teaching in a lecture hall, so that “all the people of the province of Asia, Jews and Greeks alike, heard the word of the Lord” (Acts 19:10), and of a riot in the theatre, where the crowd cried out for about two hours, “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!” When Paul later said goodbye to the Ephesian elders at Miletus, he reminded them that “for three years I did not stop, night or day, admonishing each one of you with tears” (Acts 20:31).

It is a surprise, then, that the letter sounds as though Paul has never met its readers. He has “heard of your faith” (1:15); he supposes they have heard how God entrusted him with his grace (3:2). And some of the oldest manuscripts do not have the words “in Ephesus” in the first verse at all. Many readers think the letter was meant for several churches in the province, Ephesus chief among them, and carried from one to the next. In the second century the teacher Marcion knew it as the letter “to the Laodiceans”; Tertullian, answering him, insisted that the church had always received it as written to the Ephesians. Paul tells the Colossians to read “the letter that comes from Laodicea” (Colossians 4:16), and some have wondered whether this is that letter.

Who wrote it

The letter names Paul as its author, twice (1:1; 3:1), and speaks of him as a prisoner (3:1; 4:1) and as “an ambassador, though in a chain” (6:20). It is to be carried by Tychicus (6:21), who also carries Colossians, and the two letters are so alike in shape and wording that they must be read together.

Here Christians differ. The church has always received the letter as Paul’s, probably written from prison in Rome around AD 60–62, and many scholars still hold that view. Many others think it was written after Paul’s death by a disciple who knew his letters well, pointing to its long, piled-up sentences, its vocabulary, its use of Colossians, and its picture of the church as one worldwide body rather than a congregation in a house. Readers on both sides agree on what matters most for reading it: this is Paul’s gospel, gathered up and looked at whole.

The shape of the letter

  • Chapters 1–3: what God has done. A long blessing of God for every gift in Christ; a prayer for eyes to see it; the dead made alive by grace; Jew and Gentile made one; the mystery revealed to Paul; and a second prayer, which ends in praise.
  • Chapters 4–6: how to live in it. The unity of the body and its gifts; the old self and the new; children of light; the Spirit’s fullness; wives and husbands, children and parents, slaves and masters; and the armour of God.

The hinge is the first word of chapter 4: “So”. Everything Paul asks of the church in the second half stands on what God has given it in the first.

Every blessing in Christ

In Greek, verses 3 to 14 of chapter 1 are a single breathless sentence. God “chose us in Christ” before the world was founded; he marked us out to be adopted as his own sons and daughters; in Christ we have redemption, the forgiveness of our wrongdoing; and his purpose is “to bring all things together under one head in Christ, things in heaven and things on earth.” The phrase “in Christ”, or “in him”, comes again and again. It is the key to the whole letter: every gift of God is found in union with his Son.

Then Paul turns to his Gentile readers and tells them they too have been included:

And you also are in him. You heard the message of truth, the gospel that brings you salvation, and you believed; and in him you were sealed with the Holy Spirit God had promised. The Spirit is the down payment on our inheritance, until God redeems those who are his own possession, so that his glory will be praised.

— Ephesians 1:13–14

Christians have long argued over what it means that God “chose us” and “marked us out beforehand”. In the tradition of Augustine and Calvin, this is God’s choice of particular people for salvation; in the Arminian and Wesleyan traditions, God chooses a people in Christ, and those who believe are found in him. Paul does not stop to settle it. His concern is praise: three times in the passage, everything happens so that God’s glory will be praised.

Dead, and made alive

Chapter 2 begins in the grave: “you were dead in your trespasses and sins.” Paul does not soften the picture; “we all once lived among them too”, he adds, and by nature deserved God’s wrath. Then come some of the best words in the letter: “But God is rich in mercy.” He made us alive together with Christ, raised us with him, and seated us with him in the heavenly places.

The sentence that opens this introduction follows. Salvation is by grace, through faith, and none of it comes from us; we are God’s own work. Yet it is not a salvation that leaves us idle. We were created in Christ Jesus “for good works, which God made ready in advance.” Grace is the root, and good works are the fruit, never the other way round.

The wall broken down

In the temple at Jerusalem a low stone barrier kept Gentiles out of the inner courts, with warning notices threatening death to any who went further. Paul knew it well: he was arrested in Jerusalem because some thought he had taken Trophimus, an Ephesian, past it (Acts 21:29). Now he tells Gentile believers that they, once “far away”, have been brought near:

For Christ himself is our peace. He has made the two groups into one, and has broken down the wall that divided them, the hostility between them. In his own body he set aside the law with its commandments and regulations. He did this to create in himself one new humanity out of the two, so making peace, and to reconcile both of them to God in one body through the cross, by which he put the hostility to death.

— Ephesians 2:14–16

This is the heart of the letter. The gospel does not only bring individuals to God; it makes enemies into “one new humanity”. In chapter 3 Paul calls it a mystery, hidden for ages and now revealed: that “the Gentiles are fellow heirs, members of the same body, and sharers together in the promise in Christ Jesus.” And he dares to say that through this mixed, unlikely church, God’s wisdom in all its rich variety is being shown to the powers in the heavenly places. The chapter ends in a prayer that the readers may grasp “the breadth and length and height and depth” of a love that goes beyond knowledge, and in praise:

Now to the one who is able to do all things, far beyond anything we ask or think, by the power that is at work in us, to him be glory in the church and in Christ Jesus, to every generation, for ever and ever. Amen.

— Ephesians 3:20–21

One body

Paul’s first request, now that he turns to their life together, is for unity: they are to “live in a way that is worthy of God’s call”, humble, gentle and patient, keeping the unity the Spirit gives.

There is one body and one Spirit, just as there is one hope that belongs to the call you received. There is one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all, who is over all and through all and in all.

— Ephesians 4:4–6

Unity is not sameness. The risen Christ has given gifts to his church, apostles, prophets, evangelists, shepherds and teachers, to equip all God’s holy people for the work of serving, so that the whole body grows up into its head, “as we speak the truth in love.” Then the old life is stripped off like clothing and the new self put on, and Paul gets very practical: tell the truth, “Do not let the sunset find you still angry”, work and share, speak words that build up, and forgive as God has forgiven you. “Once you were darkness itself; now, in the Lord, you are light.”

Households and the Spirit

The Spirit’s fullness, in 5:18–21, shows itself in songs, in thanksgiving, and in believers submitting to one another in the reverent fear of Christ. From there Paul speaks to each member of a household in turn: wives and husbands, children and fathers, slaves and masters. It is one of the fullest passages on marriage in the New Testament, and it ends by revealing what marriage was always a picture of: “I am speaking about Christ and the church.”

Christians read these verses in more than one way. Some hold that the husband’s headship, modelled on Christ’s self-giving love, is a lasting pattern for marriage; others hold that mutual submission (5:21) is the governing idea and that Paul is reshaping the household customs of his day from within. All agree on the startling demand made of husbands, to love their wives as Christ loved the church and handed himself over for her. The words to slaves and masters belong to a world where slavery was everywhere; it is worth noticing that Paul speaks to slaves as people answerable to Christ, and tells masters that their own Master is in heaven and shows no favouritism.

The armour of God

The letter ends on a battlefield. “Our fight is not with flesh and blood”, but with spiritual powers, and so believers are to clothe themselves in God’s complete armour: truth as a belt, righteousness as a breastplate, the gospel of peace for shoes, faith as a shield, salvation as a helmet, and the word of God as the Spirit’s sword. Much of it comes from Isaiah, where God himself puts on righteousness and the helmet of salvation (Isaiah 59:17). A prisoner chained to a Roman soldier hardly needed to look far for the picture. And the armour ends in prayer, for all God’s holy people and for Paul himself, that he may speak boldly.

How to read Ephesians

It takes about twenty minutes to read aloud, and it is worth hearing that way, as its first hearers did. Then read it slowly, a paragraph at a time.

Notice how often Paul prays, and pray his prayers (1:15–23; 3:14–21). Notice the little words “in Christ” and “in him”, and the three movements Watchman Nee summed up as sit, walk and stand: seated with Christ (2:6), living in a way worthy of God’s call (4:1), and standing your ground (6:13–14). Notice how the first half is full of what God has done and the second half of what we are to do, and do not read the commands of chapters 4 to 6 without the gifts of chapters 1 to 3 beneath them.

About this translation

The text in this edition is the Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Greek and given freely to the public domain. It is printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. A few of its choices in Ephesians are worth knowing about before you begin.

Long sentences. Paul’s Greek runs on for verse after verse in 1:3–14, 1:15–23 and 3:1–12. The translation keeps each passage together but breaks it into English sentences that can be read aloud.

“God’s holy people.” Where older Bibles say “saints”, this translation says “God’s holy people”, which is what the word means: not a few outstanding Christians, but all who belong to God.

“In Ephesus.” The translation keeps these words in 1:1, as almost all later manuscripts do and most Bibles print them, though some of the earliest leave them out.

“Let the Spirit fill you.” In 5:18 it presents the Spirit as the one who fills, and it prints verses 18 to 21 as one passage, so that the songs, the thanksgiving and the mutual submission are all seen to flow from the Spirit’s filling.

“Christ.” As elsewhere, the Open Word Bible lets a reader choose whether Christos reads “Christ” or “the Messiah”. This edition prints “Christ”, but in a letter about Gentiles being brought into Israel’s hope, it is worth remembering that the word means Israel’s anointed King.

For the reasoning behind every sentence of the translation, with the Greek beside it, see the Open Word Bible itself at openwordbible.org.

fields.title: Ephesians 1
fields.body_html:
Greeting

From Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, to God’s holy people in Ephesus, who are faithful in Christ Jesus. Grace and peace to you from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

Chosen, redeemed and sealed in Christ

Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. In Christ he has blessed us with every blessing the Spirit gives in the heavenly places. Even before the world was founded, God chose us in Christ, so that we would be holy and without blemish before him in love. He marked us out beforehand to be adopted as his own sons and daughters through Jesus Christ. That was what he gladly willed, so that his glorious grace would be praised, the grace he has freely given us in the Beloved. In him and through his blood we have redemption, the forgiveness of our wrongdoing. We have it because God’s grace is so rich, grace that he has poured out on us in abundance, with all wisdom and understanding. He has made known to us the mystery of his will, as it pleased him to do. He set out this purpose in Christ as his plan for when the times reach their fullness: to bring all things together under one head in Christ, things in heaven and things on earth, all in him. In him we too have been claimed as God’s own portion. We were marked out for this beforehand by the purpose of God, who works out everything as his will determines, so that we who were the first to hope in Christ would bring praise to his glory. And you also are in him. You heard the message of truth, the gospel that brings you salvation, and you believed; and in him you were sealed with the Holy Spirit God had promised. The Spirit is the down payment on our inheritance, until God redeems those who are his own possession, so that his glory will be praised.

Paul prays that they may know God’s power

For this reason, since I heard of your faith in the Lord Jesus and your love for all God’s holy people, I have never stopped thanking God for you. I mention you whenever I pray, asking the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, to give you the Spirit who brings wisdom and revelation as you come to know him. With the eyes of your heart opened to the light, you will know what hope his call holds out to you, how rich and glorious an inheritance he has in his holy people, and how far beyond all measure is his power at work for us who believe. It is the working of his mighty strength, which he put to work in Christ when he raised him from the dead and set him at his right hand in the heavenly places, high above every ruler and authority, every power and dominion, and every name that can be named, not only in this age but in the age to come as well. God has put all things under the feet of Christ, and has given him to the church to be head over all things. The church is his body. It is his fullness, filled by him who fills everything in every place and every way.

fields.title: Ephesians 2
fields.body_html:
From death to life

As for you, you were dead in your trespasses and sins. You once lived in them, following the way of this world in its present age and following the ruler of the realm of the air, the ruler of the spirit now at work in those who disobey. We all once lived among them too, following the desires of our flesh and doing whatever our flesh and our thoughts wanted. By nature we deserved God’s wrath, just like the rest of humanity. But God is rich in mercy. Because of the great love he had for us, even when we were dead in our trespasses, he made us alive together with Christ. You have been saved by grace. With him God raised us up, and with him seated us in the heavenly places, in Christ Jesus, so that through the ages still to come he might put on display the wealth of his grace, which surpasses all measure, seen in the kindness he has shown us in Christ Jesus. For it is by this grace that you have been saved, through faith. None of this comes from you; it is God’s gift. It is not the result of what anyone has done, so there is no room for anyone to boast. For we are God’s own work. In Christ Jesus he created us for good works, which God made ready in advance so that we would live our lives doing them.

Two peoples made one

So remember what you once were: Gentiles by birth, labeled “the uncircumcised” by those who are called “the circumcised”, a circumcision performed on the body by human hands. Remember that at that time you were without Christ. You were excluded from citizenship in Israel and were strangers to the covenants built on God’s promise. You had no hope, and you were without God in the world. But now you who were once far away are in Christ Jesus, and the blood of Christ has brought you near. For Christ himself is our peace. He has made the two groups into one, and has broken down the wall that divided them, the hostility between them. In his own body he set aside the law with its commandments and regulations. He did this to create in himself one new humanity out of the two, so making peace, and to reconcile both of them to God in one body through the cross, by which he put the hostility to death. He came with good news: peace for you who were far off, and peace for those who were near. It is through him that both of us can approach the Father, in the one Spirit. So you are no longer strangers and resident foreigners. You are citizens together with God’s holy people, and you belong to God’s household. You have been built on the apostles and prophets as your foundation, and the cornerstone is Christ Jesus himself. In him all the building, as it is fitted together, is growing into a holy temple in the Lord. And in him you also are being built up with the others into a home for God, who lives there by the Spirit.

fields.title: Ephesians 3
fields.body_html:
Paul’s task: the mystery made known

For this reason I, Paul, the prisoner of Christ Jesus for the sake of you Gentiles— surely you have heard how God entrusted me with his grace, to manage it for your good. God made the mystery known to me by revelation, as I have briefly written already. When you read this, you will be able to see my understanding of the mystery of Christ. In other generations it was not made known to humankind as it has now been revealed by the Spirit to his holy apostles and prophets. This is the mystery: through the gospel the Gentiles are fellow heirs, members of the same body, and sharers together in the promise in Christ Jesus. I became a servant of this gospel by the gift of God’s grace, which was given to me through the working of his power. Though I am less than the least of all God’s holy people, this grace was given to me: to bring the Gentiles the good news of the riches of Christ, riches no one can ever fully trace, and to make plain to everyone how the mystery is being carried out, the mystery that for ages past was hidden in God, who created all things. God’s aim was that now, through the church, his wisdom in all its rich variety would be made known to the rulers and authorities in the heavenly places. This was in keeping with the purpose he has had through all the ages, which he carried out in Christ Jesus our Lord. In him, through faith in him, we can come to God boldly and with confidence. So I ask you not to lose heart over the troubles I bear for your sake. They are your glory.

Paul kneels in prayer

For this reason I kneel before the Father, from whom every family in heaven and on earth takes its name. I pray that, in keeping with the riches of his glory, he will give you power, making your inner self strong through his Spirit, so that through faith and in love Christ will make his home in your hearts. You are rooted deep and set on a firm foundation, and I pray that you will have the strength to grasp, with all God’s holy people, the breadth and length and height and depth, and to know the love of Christ, a love that goes beyond knowledge, so that you may be filled up to all the fullness of God.

Now to the one who is able to do all things, far beyond anything we ask or think, by the power that is at work in us, to him be glory in the church and in Christ Jesus, to every generation, for ever and ever. Amen.

fields.title: Ephesians 4
fields.body_html:
Keep the unity the Spirit gives

So I, a prisoner for the Lord, appeal to you: live in a way that is worthy of God’s call, the call that came to you. Be humble and gentle in every way, and be patient, putting up with one another in love. Spare no effort to keep the unity the Spirit gives, with peace as the bond that holds you together. There is one body and one Spirit, just as there is one hope that belongs to the call you received. There is one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all, who is over all and through all and in all.

Gifts for building up the body

But grace was given to each one of us, in the measure in which Christ gave it. That is why it says, “When he went up on high, he led a band of captives, and he gave gifts to people.” Now what does “He went up” mean, if not that he had also come down into the lower parts of the earth? The one who came down is the very same one who went up, far above all the heavens, so that he might fill all things. It was he who gave some to be apostles, some prophets, some evangelists, and some shepherds and teachers. He gave them to equip God’s holy people for the work of serving, so that the body of Christ would be built up, until all of us arrive at the unity of the faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God. Then we will be a mature adult, grown to the full measure of the stature that belongs to the fullness of Christ. We will no longer be infants, thrown about by the waves and driven this way and that by each new wind of teaching, at the mercy of people who play tricks and cunningly scheme to lead others astray. Instead, as we speak the truth in love, we must grow in every respect into him, the head, Christ. From him the whole body is joined and held together by every ligament that supplies it. As each part does its own work, the body grows and builds itself up in love.

Strip off the old self, put on the new

So I tell you this, and insist on it in the Lord: you must no longer live as the Gentiles live, with their futile, empty thinking. Their understanding is darkened, and they are cut off from the life of God because of the ignorance that is in them, because their hearts have grown hard. They have lost all feeling and have given themselves over to indecency, practicing every kind of impurity with an appetite that always wants more. But that is not how you learned Christ. You surely heard him and were taught as people who belong to him, in keeping with the truth that is in Jesus. You were taught to strip off the old self, the self of your former way of life, which is being ruined by its deceitful desires; to be made new in the spirit of your minds; and to put on the new self, created in God’s likeness, in the righteousness and holiness that come from the truth.

Living as members of one another

So now that you have stripped off falsehood, each of you must tell your neighbor the truth, for we are members of one another. If you become angry, do not let it lead you into sin. Do not let the sunset find you still angry, and do not give the devil an opening. Thieves must steal no more. Instead they must work hard, doing something good with their own hands, so that they have something to share with anyone in need. Let no rotten word pass your lips. Say only what is good, what builds up and meets the need of the moment, so that your words bring grace to those who hear them. And do not grieve God’s Holy Spirit. It was with the Spirit that you were sealed, marked out for the day of redemption. Get rid of all bitterness, bursts of temper and anger, all shouting and slander, along with every kind of malice. Be kind to one another and full of compassion. Forgive each other freely, just as God has forgiven you in Christ.

fields.title: Ephesians 5
fields.body_html:
So imitate God, since you are children he dearly loves. Let love guide the way you live, as Christ loved us and handed himself over for our sake, an offering and sacrifice to God, a fragrance that pleased him.

Children of light

Sexual immorality, impurity of every kind, and greed must not even be spoken of as present among you; that is what suits God’s holy people. The same goes for shameful conduct, foolish talk and crude jokes. They do not belong. Let there be thanksgiving instead. Be sure of this, and take it to heart: no one who is sexually immoral or impure, and no one who is greedy (for the greedy person is an idolater), has any inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God.

Do not let anyone mislead you with words that have nothing in them. These are the very things that bring the wrath of God on those who disobey him. So do not become their partners in what they do. Once you were darkness itself; now, in the Lord, you are light. So conduct your lives as children of light. What light produces is goodness, righteousness and truth of every kind. Put things to the test, and learn what is pleasing to the Lord. Do not share in the deeds of darkness, which produce nothing good. Show them up for what they are instead. The things those people do in secret are shameful even to speak of. But when anything is exposed by the light, it is seen for what it is, for whatever is brought into view becomes light. So it says: “Sleeper, wake up! Get up from among the dead, and Christ will give you light.”

Live wisely, filled by the Spirit

So take great care how you live, not as people without wisdom but as people who have it. Make good use of every opportunity, because the days are evil. For this reason, do not be senseless. Come to understand what the Lord wants. Do not get drunk on wine, for that is reckless, wasteful living. Instead, let the Spirit fill you. Then you will speak to one another in psalms, hymns and Spirit-given songs, and sing and make music to the Lord with your hearts. You will give thanks to God the Father at all times and for everything, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. And you will submit to one another in the reverent fear of Christ.

Submitting to one another: wives and husbands

Wives should submit to their own husbands, as to the Lord. For the husband is head of the wife, just as Christ is head of the church; and he is the Savior of that body. But in the same way that the church submits to Christ, wives are also to submit to their husbands in everything.

Husbands, love your wives the way Christ loved the church and handed himself over for her. He did this to make her holy, cleansing her by the washing of water with the word, so that he might bring the church to himself in glory, with no spot or wrinkle or any flaw like that, but holy and without blame. So husbands are bound to love their wives as their own bodies. To love one’s wife is to love oneself. Nobody has ever hated his own flesh; instead, he feeds it and looks after it, as Christ does for the church, because we are parts of his body. This is why a man will leave his father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two will be one flesh. There is a great mystery here, but I am speaking about Christ and the church. But to return to you: each husband must love his wife as he loves himself, and the wife must see to it that she respects her husband.

fields.title: Ephesians 6
fields.body_html:
Children and parents

Children, obey your parents in the Lord, because this is right. “Honor your father and mother.” This is the first commandment that comes with a promise: “so that things may go well for you and you may enjoy a long life on the earth.”

Fathers, do not drive your children to anger. Instead, bring them up with the Lord’s training and correction.

Slaves and masters

Slaves, obey your earthly masters with fear and trembling and with an undivided heart, as you obey Christ. Do not work only while they are watching, to win their favor. Work as slaves of Christ, who do the will of God. Serve as slaves with all your heart and with goodwill, as serving the Lord and not people, because you know that the Lord will repay each one for whatever good they do, whether they are slave or free.

Masters, treat your slaves in the same way. Stop threatening them, because you know that the one who is both their Master and yours is in heaven, and he does not show favoritism.

God’s complete armor

Finally, be made strong in the Lord and in his mighty strength. Clothe yourselves in God’s complete armor, so that you can hold your ground against the devil’s cunning plans. Our fight is not with flesh and blood. It is with the rulers, with the authorities, with the world rulers of this darkness, with the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly places. For this reason, take up God’s complete armor. Then you will be able to resist on the evil day and, having carried everything through, remain standing. So stand your ground. Tie truth around your waist as a belt, and put on righteousness as your breastplate. For shoes, put on the readiness that the gospel of peace gives. In every situation take up faith as your shield; with it you will be able to put out all the burning arrows of the evil one. Receive salvation as your helmet, and the sword that the Spirit gives, which is the word of God. Pray in the Spirit at every opportunity, with every kind of prayer and request. To that end, keep watch, never giving up, and make requests for all God’s holy people. Pray also for me, that when I open my mouth I will be given the words to make known with boldness the mystery of the gospel. For its sake I am an ambassador, though in a chain. Pray that I may speak of it boldly, as I must.

Tychicus, and a closing blessing

Tychicus, our dear brother and a faithful servant in the Lord, will tell you everything, so that you too may know how I am and what I am doing. I am sending him to you for this very reason, so that you may know how we are and so that he may encourage your hearts.

Peace to the brothers and sisters, and love with faith, from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. Grace be with all who love our Lord Jesus Christ with a love that will never perish.

fields.title: Conclusion
fields.body_html:
Peace to the brothers and sisters, and love with faith, from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. Grace be with all who love our Lord Jesus Christ with a love that will never perish.

— Ephesians 6:23–24

Ephesians ends without a single name except that of the man who carries it. There are no greetings to friends, only peace, love and faith for the brothers and sisters, and grace for everyone who loves the Lord Jesus Christ with a love that will never perish. It is a fitting close for a letter about the whole church. Its last word reaches past Ephesus, past the province of Asia, to anyone, anywhere, who loves him.

The question the letter leaves

Ephesians asks what kind of people the church is. Its answer is very large. The church is Christ’s body and his fullness, the household of God, a temple still being built, a bride being made ready. Through it God’s wisdom is being shown to the powers of heaven.

And yet the church Paul knew was small and unremarkable: a few households of Jews and Gentiles who had once despised one another, slaves and masters sharing the same bread, people who still lied, lost their tempers and stole. The letter does not pretend otherwise. That is why it ends its great vision with plain commands. The question it leaves is whether the church will live as what God has made it. Will those who have been brought near keep the unity the Spirit gives? Will they speak the truth in love, and forgive as they have been forgiven? The wall has been broken down. It is all too easy to build it again.

Where the letter points

It points first to praise. Paul begins with “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ” and cannot finish his first prayer without breaking into worship. A reader who closes Ephesians with more ideas about the church, and no more love for its Lord, has missed the point.

And it points to a walk. Grace saves us apart from works, and then sets us walking in the good works God made ready in advance. The last picture in the letter is not of a church sitting still but of one standing its ground, armoured in God’s own strength and praying for those who carry the gospel.

Where to go from here

Ephesians has been a favourite of preachers and teachers in every age, and many of them are in this library. A few places to begin:

  • The first readers. Ignatius of Antioch’s letter to the same church, written about fifty years later, in The Epistles of Ignatius and His Life’s Story, which calls them “associates in the mysteries with Paul”; and Tertullian’s Against Marcion, whose fifth book defends the title “to the Ephesians”.
  • On grace through faith (chapter 2). John Wesley’s Salvation by Faith (2:8), Charles H. Spurgeon’s All of Grace, J. C. Ryle’s Living or Dead? (2:1), and John Flavel’s The Method of Grace, with sermons on 1:6, 1:7 and 2:1.
  • On Paul’s prayers (chapters 1 and 3). Dwight L. Moody’s The Way to God, whose first chapter, “Love That Passeth Knowledge”, takes up 3:19; and Devoted to Prayer, with a chapter on each prayer, “That You May Know Him Better” and “Rooted Deep in Love”.
  • On the Spirit (chapters 4 and 5). Robert Murray M’Cheyne’s Grieve Not the Holy Spirit (4:30) and Charles G. Finney’s Be Filled with the Spirit (5:18).
  • On sitting, walking and standing. The Key Teachings of Watchman Nee, whose chapters “Sit”, “Walk” and “Stand” follow Nee’s reading of the whole letter; John Wesley’s sermon Of the Church (4:1–6), in his Sermons on Several Occasions; and Andrew Murray’s Abide in Christ, whose chapter “As Your Strength” is on 6:10.

You can also go the other way, from the text to the classics. Every reference to Ephesians in this library can be tapped to read the verse, and the Scripture pages gather, chapter by chapter, what the great writers of the church have said about each passage of this letter.

But the best next step may be to read Ephesians again, and to pray its two prayers for your own church, by name. And when you come to the end, hear its first command for the battle as spoken to you:

Finally, be made strong in the Lord and in his mighty strength.

— Ephesians 6:10
